tier_reason: README 'Library Comparisons' tables match every claimed number (FastNoise Lite, FastNoise legacy, libnoise, stb perlin rows) and state CPU (Intel 7820X @ 4.9 GHz), compiler (clang-cl 10.0.0) and flags (-m64 /O2); the harness is public in Auburn/NoiseBenchmarking (main.cpp, FastNoise2/Benchmark_FastNoise2.cpp, FastNoiseLite/Benchmark_FastNoiseLite.cpp, Google Benchmark submodule).

corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang-cl 10.0.0 -m64 /O2 (README); the harness's CMakeSettings.json release configuration (x64-Clang-Release) is RelWithDebInfo
corrections.caveats: Benchmark harness is the author's own Auburn/NoiseBenchmarking repo (6 stars, 14 commits, last commit 2020-09-15; no results file checked in) and pins the FastNoise2 submodule at commit e191bc2 from September 2020, so the README table describes a six-year-old version of the library, not current master (which keeps receiving correctness fixes, e.g. CellularDistance double sqrt fixed 2026-10-09). The comparison is FastNoise2's bulk GenUniformGrid2D/3D into an array (AVX2 level forced) against per-point GetNoise calls wrapped in benchmark::DoNotOptimize for FastNoise Lite and the other scalar libraries, so the gain mixes SIMD and API-shape effects. The 3D 'Simplex' column compares FastNoise2's Simplex node with FastNoise Lite's OpenSimplex2 (marked with an asterisk); against the like-for-like FastNoise legacy Simplex (44.74) the 3D ratio is 6.0x (derived from page data). The author's earlier SIMD library FastNoiseSIMD is built by the harness but omitted from the README table, so no SIMD competitor is shown. Frequencies differ (0.02 for FastNoise2, FastNoise Lite default for the others). Old compiler (clang-cl 10) on Windows, single machine. The continuous-benchmark page on auburn.github.io was not reachable here.

notes: Numbers and ratios (about 4.2x to 7.7x) verified on the README; tier A holds because the harness code, compiler, flags and CPU are all public, but the table is from a 2020 FastNoise2 snapshot and the Simplex column is not like-for-like against FastNoise Lite. Record shortcomings: stale 2020 numbers, bulk SIMD API vs per-point scalar API, OpenSimplex2 vs Simplex mismatch, first-party harness.

tier_reason: README speedup tables (vs auto-vectorized pospopcnt_u16_scalar_naive and vs pospopcnt_u16_scalar_naive_nosimd) contain every claimed figure, name the CPU (Core i3-8121U) and compiler (GCC 7.3.1), and the public Makefile sets -O3 -march=native; benchmark code is benchmark.cpp (checks every method against scalar_naive each iteration via assert_truth). The method is also in a peer-reviewed paper (Concurrency and Computation: Practice and Experience 33(17), 2021).

corrections.workload: Positional population count (set-bit counts at each of 16 bit positions) over arrays of 16-bit values; the speedup tables cover arrays of 128 to 65536 values on one core, while the cycles-per-integer and MB/s tables use 1 million uniformly random simulated FLAG fields over 1,000 repetitions.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 57 stars; code of the paper 'Efficient Computation of Positional Population Counts Using SIMD Instructions' (Klarqvist, Muła, Lemire), Concurrency and Computation: Practice and Experience 33(17), 2021, DOI 10.1002/cpe.6304 (venue from search snippet; arXiv 1911.02696); README points production users to libalgebra
corrections.caveats: Speedup-table baseline is the compiler auto-vectorized scalar version at -O3 -march=native, a fair baseline; the 138.71x figure is against a deliberately non-vectorized baseline. Speedup table comes from one 2019-era laptop-class Cannon Lake CPU; the AVX-512 paths do not run on most AMD or client Intel parts of that era. The README tables predate the final code: the cycles and MB/s tables list methods (pospopcnt_u16_avx512_csa, avx2_csa, mula3) that no longer exist under those names in pospopcnt.c, and the speedup table's avx512_adder_forest/blend names are now avx512bw_*. Timing uses CPUID/RDTSC serialization per call and the input is regenerated and pre-touched by the reference function before each timed call, so small-array (128-512 values) ratios include fixed overhead and warm-cache effects. Peer-reviewed in CCPE 2021 (venue from search snippet only; arXiv not reachable). libalgebra (same author) reuses these kernels, so the two entries overlap; a follow-up paper (arXiv 2412.16370, Clausecker, Lemire, Schintke) extends the method to AVX2, AVX-512 and ASIMD.

notes: All claimed numbers verified on the README; tier A stands (public benchmark.cpp + Makefile flags + GCC 7.3.1 + Core i3-8121U), plus peer-reviewed CCPE 2021 paper. Shortcomings: abandoned since 2020-01-23, single Cannon Lake machine, README tables predate method renames, AVX-512-only headline. Lead: arXiv 2412.16370 follow-up (Clausecker/Lemire/Schintke) may have its own repo.

tier_reason: README benchmark output matches every claimed time (scalar 103 ms; sizes 8/16/32/64 at 28.0/16.2/12.5/10.9 ms; 128 at 158 ms) and states clang++ 9.0, -O3 -march=native, Core i7-9750H; the benchmark code is public (benchmark/shader.cpp with example/shader.cpp, CMakeLists.txt sets -O3 -march=native) and test/shader.cpp checks every vector size against the scalar output.

corrections.workload: Per-pixel integer shader over a 512x512 int screen buffer (99 iterations of multiply and modulo-by-constant integer arithmetic per pixel), pure_simd_shader instantiated with vector sizes 1 to 128, against the same loop written in plain scalar C++.
corrections.caveats: A single toy workload (one shader adapted from the 'Practical SIMD Programming' tutorial) on one laptop CPU; the scalar baseline is the author's own loop with the same flags. Its inner loop is a serial 99-step dependency chain per pixel, so the gain comes from the compiler SLP-vectorizing the unrolled independent pixels, while the scalar loop as written evidently was not vectorized (it ties vector size 1 at 103 ms) and size 128 is 1.5x slower (158 ms). The shader relies on signed 32-bit overflow (px*py terms exceed INT_MAX), which is undefined behaviour in both versions; outputs match in the repo's test. The second benchmark (benchmark/sum.cpp) has no published results. Numbers are aggregate means of 10 repetitions. No comparison with Highway, xsimd, Eigen or std::simd; the README calls the library experimental with unstable interfaces.

notes: Numbers verified; tier A holds on public benchmark code, compiler, flags and CPU, and the test confirms equal outputs. Shortcomings: one toy shader, author-written scalar baseline, signed-overflow UB in the workload, no comparison against other SIMD libraries, abandoned since 2021-10-04.
